name: Parallel Sub-Agents with Isolated Context
question: How do I run many pieces at once without flooding one context?
summary: An orchestrator splits a job into independent pieces and starts one sub-agent per piece, all at the same time. Each sub-agent gets a fresh, isolated context window holding only its brief, does its own reading and tool calls, and returns a condensed result, such as a card of at most 500 tokens, instead of its transcript. Anthropic’s multi-agent research system works this way. This page covers the fan-out and fan-in mechanics: concurrency, condensed returns, shared inputs and the merge check. Whether to split at all is Single vs Multi-Agent; how workers are briefed and tool-scoped is Supervisor and Workers.
useCases: Comparing many independent entities at once, such as 12 companies’ quarterly results
Broad research across sources that together overflow one context window
Batch reviews where each item can be judged on its own: loan files, claims, contracts

items.detail: one sub-agent per independent piece, started together under a concurrency cap
each sub-agent sees its brief and its own tool results, nothing else
a fixed schema of at most about 500 tokens per item, not the transcript
the slowest sub-agent plus planning and merging, not the sum of all
every sub-agent pays its own prompt, tools and reasoning, so the total rises with fan-out
the fan-in step that compares shared figures, units and gaps before synthesis

steps: Split the job into pieces that share no inputs; compute any shared input once and put it in every brief
Start one fresh session per piece, all at once, under a concurrency and budget cap
Have each return a validated card of at most about 500 tokens, with its sources
Fan in through a merge check: same shared figures, same units, no gaps, conflicts flagged
pitfalls: Each sub-agent re-derives a shared input, so work is duplicated and findings conflict
Returning transcripts refills the orchestrator’s context that isolation was meant to protect
Awaiting sub-agents one by one in a loop quietly makes the fan-out sequential
remember: Fan out the independent, pass shared inputs in, bring back cards, check before merging.
caption: Illustrative: 12 pharma companies at Dalal Lens Research, a fictional equity-research firm; 40k tokens of filings each, 40k of overhead per sub-agent, a 200k window, ₹0.40 per 1,000 tokens.

comparison.scope: How parallel pieces run and come back
comparison.needs: Independent pieces and a return schema

code.text: from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage
SECTOR = {"usd_inr": 86.4, "api_price_index": 112.0}   # computed ONCE, sent to all
class Card(BaseModel):                     # what comes back: at most ~500 tokens
revenue_cr: float                      # ₹ crore, one unit for everyone
BRIEF = """Analyse {co} only, from the files in this folder.
Use these sector figures exactly; do not re-derive them: {sector}
Reply with JSON only, matching this schema, in under 500 tokens: {schema}"""
async def analyse(co: str, sem: asyncio.Semaphore) -> Card:
async with sem:                                   # at most 6 at once
cwd=f"./filings/{co}",                    # sees only its own folder
async for msg in query(prompt=prompt, options=opts):   # new session, fresh context
return Card.model_validate_json(msg.result)   # the card, not the transcript
got = await asyncio.gather(*(analyse(c, sem) for c in names),
return_exceptions=True)   # one failure is not all
cards = {c: r for c, r in zip(names, got) if isinstance(r, Card)}
return cards, [c for c in names if c not in cards]
retried, missing = await fan_out(missing)    # retry once, then report

steps.title: One fresh session per company
steps.text: Every query() call starts a new session with its own context window. The sub-agent for Kaveri sees its brief and the files in ./filings/Kaveri, nothing from the other eleven, and its 40k tokens of filings never leave that session.

steps.title: Pass shared inputs in, once
steps.text: All twelve comparisons depend on the same USD/INR rate and API price index. The orchestrator computes them once and writes them into every brief. Left alone, twelve sub-agents would each look them up again: eleven duplicate reads and up to eleven different rates.

steps.title: Fan out under a cap
steps.text: asyncio.gather starts all twelve and Semaphore(6) lets six run at a time, so they go in two waves: the wall-clock is about two company-lengths, not twelve. max_turns and max_budget_usd bound each session’s spend.

steps.title: Return a card, not a transcript
steps.text: Only the final ResultMessage comes back, validated as a Card of under 500 tokens with its sources. Twelve cards are 6k tokens; twelve transcripts of about 80k each would be 960k, far beyond the orchestrator’s window.

steps.title: Expect failures
steps.text: return_exceptions=True means one session that times out or returns bad JSON does not throw away the other eleven. Missing companies are retried once and then reported by name, never silently dropped.

steps.title: Merge check before synthesis
steps.text: Fan-in checks that every card used the same USD/INR rate and the same units, and lists conflicts and gaps. The orchestrator then holds about 14k tokens: 2k of its own, 6k of briefs and 6k of cards.

pros: Wall-clock falls to about the slowest piece plus planning and merging
Each sub-agent’s context holds only its piece, so nothing overflows
Raw reading stays in the sub-agents; the orchestrator sees only cards
Breadth: many entities or sources covered in one run
cons: Tokens rise with every sub-agent, because each pays its own prompt, tools and reasoning
Shared inputs re-derived per sub-agent cause duplicated work and conflicting figures
A condensed card can drop a detail the synthesis needed
More moving parts: concurrency caps, rate limits, retries and partial failures
avoidWhen: The pieces are tightly coupled, such as one valuation model or one refactor: keep one agent
The job fits one context and nobody is waiting on the minutes saved: one agent is cheaper

playgroundGuide.scenario: Dalal Lens Research, a fictional equity-research firm, compares 12 pharma companies on results day. Each company has 40k tokens of filings and takes 10 minutes to analyse. Every sub-agent adds 40k tokens of overhead and 3 minutes to start, a context window holds 200k tokens, and tokens cost ₹0.40 per 1,000. The orchestrator plans for 2 minutes and uses 2k tokens plus 0.5k per brief.
controls: Choose how many sub-agents to start: 1, 3, 6 or 12.
Choose whether each returns its full transcript or a condensed card of at most 500 tokens per company, and whether the companies share inputs.
Turn the orchestrator’s merge check on or off.

outputs.name: Wall-clock
outputs.meaning: Planning, the slowest sub-agent’s companies at 10 minutes each, start-up, any shared lookups, merging and the merge check.

outputs.name: Total tokens · cost
outputs.meaning: Every sub-agent’s context plus the orchestrator’s, at ₹0.40 per 1,000 tokens.

outputs.name: Orchestrator context
outputs.meaning: Its own plan and briefs, everything the sub-agents return, and the merge check.

outputs.name: Coverage
outputs.meaning: How much of each sub-agent’s work fits its 200k window, times how much of what comes back fits the orchestrator’s.

outputs.name: Conflicting findings
outputs.meaning: Companies judged on different sector figures from the others, when each sub-agent works them out itself.

presets.name: Transcripts, shared inputs
presets.expect: 3 sub-agents return full transcripts and each looks up the sector figures itself: 58 minutes, 1,293.5k tokens (₹517), the orchestrator holds 603.5k tokens, coverage 28% and 8 of 12 companies conflict.

presets.name: 12 sub-agents, no check
presets.expect: 12 sub-agents returning cards finish in 22 minutes with 100% coverage and a 14k orchestrator, but 1,334k tokens (₹534), 330k of it duplicated lookups, and 11 of 12 companies conflict.

presets.name: 6 sub-agents with a merge check
presets.expect: The merge check reconciles all 10 conflicts, so 0 remain and coverage is 100%, but it takes 35 minutes, 935k tokens (₹374) and a 35k orchestrator context.

presets.name: One agent
presets.expect: One agent does all 12 companies: 127 minutes, 528.5k tokens (₹211), no conflicts, but its 520k tokens of work in a 200k window give only 38% coverage.

missions.text: Finish in 30 minutes or less with 100% coverage, no conflicting findings and an orchestrator context of 20k tokens or less.
missions.hint: Make the companies independent by passing the sector figures in every brief, return cards, and use 6 or 12 sub-agents.

missions.text: Keep the shared dependencies, but get to 0 conflicting findings in under 30 minutes.
missions.hint: The merge check reconciles conflicts; with 12 sub-agents returning cards it finishes in 25 minutes.
Fewer sub-agents pay less overhead: 3 sub-agents on independent tasks returning cards cost about ₹244.

tools.best: Sub-agents defined in code, each with its own prompt, tool list and model, called through the Agent tool.
tools.ex: A research orchestrator fans out one read-only sub-agent per company filing and merges their summaries.
cons: Sub-agent spawning must be bounded deliberately

tools.best: Map-reduce fan-out inside a graph: one Send per item, each worker gets only its slice, a reducer collects the results.
tools.ex: One Send per company to an analyse node; operator.add gathers the cards for a merge node.
pros: Parallel branches and reducers are explicit
max_concurrency caps the fan-out in the run config
cons: You write the merge and conflict checks

tools.best: A workflow agent that runs its sub-agents concurrently, each on its own branch of the conversation.
tools.ex: Three research sub-agents run at once, each writing to its own output_key, then a merge agent reads them.
pros: Parallel run in a few lines
Pairs with SequentialAgent for fan-out then merge
cons: Sub-agents share session state, so writes need distinct keys

tools.best: Code-driven fan-out: run several agents with Runner.run concurrently and merge their final outputs yourself.
tools.ex: Twelve Runner.run calls, one per company, gathered with a semaphore and merged into one table.
pros: Deterministic fan-out you control in code
cons: Concurrency caps and retries are your job

A few lines of parallel workflow on Google’s stack

goals: Explain why parallel sub-agents save minutes but cost more tokens
Pass shared inputs in the brief instead of letting each sub-agent re-derive them
Design a condensed return and a merge check for the fan-in

practice.scenario: Dalal Lens Research, a fictional equity-research firm in Mumbai, publishes a comparison of 12 listed pharma companies on the morning their quarterly results come out. The orchestrator works out the sector figures once (USD/INR and an API price index), then fans out one isolated sub-agent per company. Each reads only its company’s filings and returns a card of at most 500 tokens; a merge check confirms every card used the same figures and units before the note is written.

industries.use: One sub-agent per company on results day, cards merged into one comparison table
Parallel review of independent claim files, each returning a structured verdict with evidence
Sanctions, adverse-media and registry checks per customer run at once, merged into one risk card

practice.analogy: An exam hall with 12 examiners. Each marks one bundle of answer sheets in a separate room and hands back a one-page mark sheet, not the scripts. The chief examiner sets the marking scheme once for everyone, then checks that every mark sheet used it before publishing results.

library.name: LangGraph
library.what: Its Send API does map-reduce: a conditional edge returns one Send per item, each worker node receives only its own slice of state, and a reducer such as operator.add collects the results.

practice.note: analyse_company() is a stub for your own model call (any SDK). LangGraph runs the Send branches in the same superstep, in parallel; cap concurrency with the max_concurrency key in the run config if your model provider rate-limits you.

samples.code:
import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import Send

SECTOR = {"usd_inr": 86.4, "api_price_index": 112.0}      # computed once

class Research(TypedDict):
    companies: list[str]
    cards: Annotated[list[dict], operator.add]              # reducer: parallel writes append

class One(TypedDict):                                       # a worker sees only this
    company: str
    sector: dict

def analyse_company(company: str, sector: dict) -> dict:
    """Stub: call your model with the brief and this company's filings only."""
    return {"company": company, "revenue_cr": 0.0, "usd_inr_used": sector["usd_inr"],
            "red_flags": [], "sources": [f"filings/{company}/q2.pdf"]}

def fan_out(state: Research):
    return [Send("analyse", {"company": c, "sector": SECTOR}) for c in state["companies"]]

def analyse(slice_: One):
    card = analyse_company(slice_["company"], slice_["sector"])
    return {"cards": [card]}                                # a short card, not a transcript

def merge_check(state: Research):
    rates = {c["usd_inr_used"] for c in state["cards"]}
    seen = {c["company"] for c in state["cards"]}
    missing = [c for c in state["companies"] if c not in seen]
    return {"cards": [{"merge_check": {"conflicting_rates": sorted(rates) if len(rates) > 1 else [],
                                       "missing": missing}}]}

g = StateGraph(Research)
g.add_node("analyse", analyse)
g.add_node("merge_check", merge_check)
g.add_conditional_edges(START, fan_out, ["analyse"])
g.add_edge("analyse", "merge_check")
g.add_edge("merge_check", END)
app = g.compile()

names = ["Arogya", "Sanjivani", "Nilgiri", "Kaveri", "Vindhya", "Tapti",
         "Sahyadri", "Narmada", "Godavari", "Aravalli", "Konkan", "Chambal"]
out = app.invoke({"companies": names, "cards": []}, config={"max_concurrency": 6})
print(len(out["cards"]), out["cards"][-1])

numericDrill.question: An orchestrator fans out 12 company analyses, one isolated session each, with a concurrency cap of 4. Every session takes 10 minutes. Planning takes 2 minutes and the merge check 3 minutes. What is the wall-clock time, in minutes?
numericDrill.answer: With 4 at a time, the 12 sessions run in 12 ÷ 4 = 3 waves of 10 minutes: 30 minutes. Add 2 for planning and 3 for the merge check: 2 + 30 + 3 = 35 minutes. Run one after another they would take 2 + 120 + 3 = 125 minutes; the token bill is the same either way.

interview.question: Why should a sub-agent return a condensed card rather than its transcript?
interview.answer: The point of an isolated context is that raw reading stays with the sub-agent. A card of a few hundred tokens with a fixed schema and sources lets the orchestrator hold 12 results in about 6k tokens; 12 transcripts would be hundreds of thousands of tokens, overflow its window and make the merge worse.

interview.question: Two sub-agents report different USD/INR rates for the same quarter. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: The companies were not truly independent: each sub-agent re-derived a shared input. Compute the shared figures once in the orchestrator and pass them in every brief, record the figure each card used, and run a merge check that flags any card that differs.

mistakes.mistake: Don’t let every sub-agent look up the same shared input.
mistakes.fix: Compute it once and pass it in the brief; the merge check confirms everyone used it.

mistakes.mistake: Don’t await sub-agents one by one in a loop.
mistakes.fix: Start them together with gather or a TaskGroup, under a semaphore that caps concurrency.

quiz.question: Dalal Lens Research, a fictional equity-research firm, runs 12 sub-agents, one per company, and each reads about 40k tokens of filings. What should each sub-agent send back to the orchestrator?
options: Its full transcript, so nothing is lost
A condensed card of at most about 500 tokens in a fixed schema, with sources
Nothing: it should write straight into the final report
The raw PDFs it read, so the orchestrator can check them
quiz.explanation: The raw reading should stay inside each isolated context. Twelve cards cost about 6k tokens in the orchestrator; twelve transcripts would be about 480k tokens of filings alone.

quiz.question: An orchestrator uses 2k tokens of its own plus 0.5k per brief. It fans out 16 sub-agents, and each returns a 0.5k card. How large is the orchestrator’s context after fan-in?
options: 10k tokens
18k tokens
26k tokens
16k tokens
quiz.explanation: 2k own + 16 × 0.5k of briefs + 16 × 0.5k of cards = 2 + 8 + 8 = 18k tokens.

quiz.question: An insurer fans out 30 independent claim reviews with a concurrency cap of 10. Each review takes 6 minutes, planning takes 1 minute and merging 2 minutes. What is the wall-clock time?
options: 21 minutes
180 minutes
9 minutes
183 minutes
quiz.explanation: Thirty reviews at 10 at a time run in 3 waves of 6 minutes: 18 minutes. Add 1 for planning and 2 for merging: 21 minutes. Run one by one they would take 1 + 180 + 2 = 183 minutes.

quiz.question: A payments company plans to fan out dispute analysis across many sub-agents. Which are real costs of that design? (Select all that apply.)
options: More total tokens, because every sub-agent pays its own prompt, tools and reasoning
Coordination work: concurrency caps, retries and partial failures
Conflicting results when the pieces secretly share an input
A longer wall-clock than doing the disputes one by one
quiz.explanation: Fan-out saves wall-clock time, so the last option is wrong. It does cost tokens, coordination and the risk of conflicting findings when pieces are not truly independent.

quiz.question: A clinical support agent must adjust one patient’s medication plan, where every dose change affects the others. A developer proposes one parallel sub-agent per drug. What is the better design?
options: Keep it with one agent, because the decisions are tightly coupled
Twelve sub-agents, one per drug, to finish faster
Sub-agents that return transcripts so the orchestrator sees everything
Sub-agents with a higher temperature for more variety
quiz.explanation: Parallel sub-agents fit independent pieces. Coupled decisions split across isolated contexts produce conflicting implicit choices, so one agent with full context is safer and cheaper.

quiz.question: An e-commerce team’s fan-out code reads: for sku in skus: results.append(await check(sku)). Fifty checks of 1 minute each take 50 minutes. Why?
options: The semaphore is too small
Each await finishes before the next check starts, so the checks run one at a time
The model is rate-limited to one call a minute
The results list is shared between sub-agents
quiz.explanation: Awaiting inside the loop makes the fan-out sequential. Start all checks together with asyncio.gather or a TaskGroup, under a concurrency cap.

quiz.question: A telecom operator fans out 12 regional churn analyses. Each sub-agent estimates the national churn baseline itself, and the regional reports disagree. What is the best fix?
options: Add a debate round between the 12 sub-agents
Compute the baseline once in the orchestrator and pass it in every brief
Return full transcripts so the orchestrator can spot the difference
Use a larger model for each sub-agent
quiz.explanation: The regions were not independent: they shared a hidden input. Computing it once removes both the duplicated work and the source of the conflict; a merge check can then confirm everyone used it.

quiz.question: Udaan Lend, a fictional NBFC, fans out loan-file reviews to sub-agents. What belongs in each sub-agent’s condensed card? (Select all that apply.)
options: A fixed schema of the key fields, such as income, obligations and red flags
The document ids behind each claim
The shared figures and units it used, such as the policy rate and ₹ lakh
Every tool call and intermediate thought
quiz.explanation: A card should be short, structured, sourced and state the shared inputs it relied on so the merge check can compare cards. Intermediate thoughts belong in the sub-agent’s own context and traces.

quiz.question: Six sub-agents each process 120k tokens and the orchestrator processes 11k. Tokens cost ₹0.40 per 1,000. What does the run cost?
Three sub-agents under a Google ADK ParallelAgent all save their results to the same session-state key, and only one result survives. What is the fix?
options: Ask the sub-agents to write shorter results
Give each sub-agent its own output_key and merge the keys afterwards
Increase the model’s context window
Ask the sub-agents to agree on one answer
quiz.explanation: Sub-agents under a ParallelAgent share session state, so writes to one key overwrite each other. Distinct output keys, read by a merge step, keep every result.

quiz.question: Twelve company sessions are started with asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True), and one times out. What does the orchestrator get back?
options: Nothing: gather raises and all results are lost
Eleven results plus the exception object in the failed company’s slot
Twelve results, with the timed-out one filled in by the model
Only the results that finished before the timeout
quiz.explanation: With return_exceptions=True, exceptions are returned in place instead of raised, so the other eleven cards survive and the missing company can be retried and reported.

quiz.question: A law firm’s data room holds 200 contracts of about 6k tokens each. Each sub-agent has a 200k window and needs 40k for its own prompt, tools and notes. What is the smallest number of sub-agents that lets every contract be read in full?
quiz.explanation: Each sub-agent has 200k − 40k = 160k for contracts, which is 26 whole contracts of 6k. 200 ÷ 26 ≈ 7.7, so 8 sub-agents are needed.

quiz.question: Anthropic reported how many tokens its multi-agent research system uses compared with ordinary chat. Roughly what multiple?
options: About 1.5×
About 4×
About 15×
About 100×
quiz.explanation: Anthropic reported single agents using about 4× the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about 15×, which is why fan-out suits valuable, broad tasks.

quiz.question: In Anthropic’s analysis of its research system on the BrowseComp benchmark, which factor alone explained most of the variance in performance?
options: Token usage
The number of sub-agents
The length of the system prompt
The sampling temperature
quiz.explanation: Token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance; together with the number of tool calls and the model choice it explained about 95%. Parallel sub-agents help partly because they spend more tokens across separate contexts.

quiz.question: A bank runs KYC refresh checks for thousands of customers with fan-out. Which practices keep this safe at scale? (Select all that apply.)
options: A concurrency cap, such as a semaphore sized to the provider’s rate limits
A turn or budget cap on every session
Retrying failed pieces once, then reporting what is still missing
Letting every sub-agent start more sub-agents without a limit
quiz.explanation: Caps on concurrency and per-session spend, plus explicit handling of failures, keep a large fan-out predictable. Unbounded nested spawning multiplies cost and failure modes.

quiz.question: One agent analyses 10 regions at 9 minutes each, then merges for 2 minutes. Ten parallel sub-agents each take 9 minutes after a 3-minute start-up, then the merge takes 2 minutes. How many minutes does the parallel design save?
quiz.explanation: One agent: 10 × 9 + 2 = 92 minutes. Parallel: 3 + 9 + 2 = 14 minutes. Saved: 92 − 14 = 78 minutes.

quiz.question: An orchestrator summarising reviews for 50 products runs out of context after the sub-agents finish. Each sub-agent returned its whole conversation. What should change?
options: Use fewer products
Have each sub-agent return a short, fixed-format card instead of its conversation
Give the orchestrator a higher temperature
Let the sub-agents share one context window
quiz.explanation: Returning transcripts brings all the raw reading back into the one context that isolation was meant to protect. Condensed cards keep fan-in small.

quiz.question: When is parallel fan-out a poor fit? (Select all that apply.)
options: The pieces are tightly coupled, so each change affects the others
The whole job fits comfortably in one context and nobody is waiting on the minutes
The pieces are independent and together overflow one window
Each piece needs the finished results of the others before it can start
quiz.explanation: Fan-out pays when pieces are independent and too big for one context. Coupled or sequential pieces, or small jobs, are cheaper and more coherent with one agent.

quiz.question: Two sub-agents in a UPI dispute review both analysed the same 400 transactions, because one was briefed on “March disputes” and the other on “high-value disputes”. What prevents this?
options: Briefs that partition the work on one key, such as non-overlapping date ranges, plus a merge check that removes duplicates by transaction id
A larger context window for each sub-agent
Returning transcripts so the orchestrator can compare them
A higher concurrency cap
quiz.explanation: Overlapping scopes cause duplicated work. Partition the pieces on a single key so they cannot overlap, and deduplicate by id at fan-in in case they still do.

quiz.question: A hospital’s orchestrator uses 4k tokens of its own. Eight sub-agents would each return a 90k transcript, or a 1k card instead. How many tokens does condensing save in the orchestrator’s context?
options: 8k
quiz.explanation: Transcripts: 4 + 8 × 90 = 724k. Cards: 4 + 8 × 1 = 12k. Saved: 724 − 12 = 712k tokens.
